docs.title: CMBLensing.py
docs.text:
CMBLensing.py is the JAX port of the Julia package CMBLensing.jl. With it you can:

  • Simulate flat-sky CMB temperature and polarization fields, lensing potentials and noisy lensed data maps (load_sim).
  • Lens, inverse-lens and adjoint-lens fields with the LenseFlow ODE (lense_flow).
  • Reconstruct the unlensed field and the lensing potential by joint MAP optimization (map_joint).
  • Sample the LCDM parameters jointly with the field and the lensing potential by Gibbs sampling (sample_joint), extending the algorithm developed by Millea et al. 2020.
  • Forecast the sampler's posterior widths with a Gaussian Fisher forecast (fisher_forecast).

All array operations run in JAX (float64), so the code runs on CPU and GPU and is differentiable where it needs to be.

docs.title: Analyzing Chain Data¶
docs.text:
sample_joint writes one history file per sampled parameter and chain. cmb_lensing/chain_analysis.py turns a directory of those files into MCMC diagnostics and plots, and can compare the measured posterior with a Fisher forecast. This notebook walks through its Python API on chains from the project's Hugging Face dataset (see Data Availability), which the first cell downloads (about 17 MB), then shows the equivalent terminal commands.

The data: 10 simulated temperature maps (\(128 \times 128\) pixels, \(\theta_\mathrm{pix} = 2.5'\), \(2.5\,\mu\)K-arcmin white noise), 5 chains per map of 6000 sweeps each, sampling \(\Omega_c h^2\), \(100\,\theta_\mathrm{MC}\) and \(\ln(10^{10} A_s)\). The run's settings are listed with its figures on the data visualizer located here.

docs.title: 1. The input: a directory of history files¶
docs.text: Each file is named <param>_map_<map seed>_chain_<chain index>_history.txt and holds one value per sweep. find_history_files lists what a directory contains. Nothing else has to be specified: the sampled parameters, the maps and the chains per map are all read off the file names.

docs.title: 2. Convergence and mixing¶
docs.text:
These are computed from the unthinned post-burn-in chains.

  • gelman_rubin_per_map: the Gelman-Rubin \(\hat{R}\) across each map's sub-chains. Values near 1 mean the sub-chains agree.
  • metropolis_acceptance_rate: the fraction of sweeps in which the parameter moved (the sampler is tuned toward about 44%).
  • autocorrelation and integrated_autocorrelation_time (from cmb_lensing.mcmc_diagnostics): how many sweeps separate two roughly independent samples.

docs.title: 3. One parameter at a time¶
docs.text:
per_param_analysis writes every single-parameter plot into a folder and returns the summary numbers. Before plotting it thins each sub-chain by its own integrated autocorrelation time (should_thin = False turns that off) and pools each map's sub-chains, so that a map's samples are nearly independent.

Each map's posterior is taken to be a normal distribution with the mean and standard deviation of that map's thinned samples. These normals are the curves of the per-map posteriors plot. The product distribution is their renormalized product, which is the inverse-variance weighted combination of the maps: the posterior one would get from all 10 maps together. Its mean should sit within about one product standard deviation of the truth; the z-score is (truth − product mean) / product std.

The product mean, std and z-score carry Monte Carlo errors from a bootstrap. Each of the 200 replicates resamples every map's thinned samples with replacement, rebuilds the normals and their product, and forms its own z-score. The errors are written in brackets, in units of the last digit: 0.1092(1) means \(0.1092 \pm 0.0001\).

The summary also holds the average over the maps of the single-map z-scores, (truth − map mean) / map std, with its standard error over maps (avg_map_z_score, avg_map_z_error). Unlike the bootstrap errors, this error includes the scatter between maps, so the average per-map z-score tests the bias directly. For well-calibrated posteriors the single-map z-scores are draws from a unit normal, so their standard deviation, which is printed, should be close to 1.

docs.title: 4. The joint posterior¶
docs.text: get_avg_covariance_matrix computes one covariance matrix per map (its unthinned sub-chains concatenated) and averages them over maps. Samples from different maps are never pooled: each map has its own posterior mean, and pooling would add the scatter of those means to the widths. The errors are a delete-one-map jackknife.

docs.title: 5. Everything at once: main¶
docs.text:
chain_analysis.main runs all of the above for every sampled parameter and writes the joint plots. By default the output goes to <chain_dir>/chain_analysis_output/; here it goes to a temporary folder. pol ("I", "P" or "IP") records which data the chains saw and only labels the plots: the chain analysis itself is the same for temperature, polarization and joint runs.

joint_information/z_scores.png is one table with a row per sampled parameter. Its columns are the product mean, std and z-score with their bootstrap errors, the average per-map z-score with its standard error, the mean and standard deviation over maps of the Gelman-Rubin \(\hat{R}\), and the burn-in.

docs.title: 6. Comparing with the Fisher forecast¶
docs.text: The forecast is off unless run_fisher = True. It is the Fisher forecast for the chains' pol, with white noise and no beam, and it carries no error bars. It needs a merged delensed_covariance.npz (see Computing Delensed Covariance Matrices), measured at the chains' box, noise level and pol, which supplies its field blocks. There is no fallback: asking for the forecast without the file is an error. The chains here saw temperature data, so pol = "I"; for "P" or "IP" chains pass that pol and a delensed covariance measured at it (include_bb = False then leaves the delensed B modes out of the forecast).

docs.text:
The following notebook goes through a worked example of how to run the synthetic data generation code, gravitationally lense the output fields, and then run the MAP estimation algorithm map_joint which finds the point estimates of (f, phi) which minimize the MSE loss between a given observed data field and the reconstructed data field with the code's forward model.

In [1]: Copied! 
from cmb_lensing.simulate import *
from cmb_lensing.statistics import *
from cmb_lensing.util import *
from cmb_lensing.wiener_filter import *
from cmb_lensing.map_joint import *
from cmb_lensing.lense_flow import *
from cmb_lensing.gradients import *

The load_sim() method from the simulate sub-module allows the user to generate a data_set object which contains unlensed CMB temperature and polarization fields, the corresponding lensed fields, the lensing potential, "data" fields which represent the lensed fields with a mask and beam applied along with instrumental noise, and all the other covariance matrices and operators that will be necessary for CMB Lensing and field estimation.

In [2]: Copied! 
#Generate an IP data set
data_set = load_sim(nside = 256, #Number of pixels per map side in real space
                    theta_pix = 2, #Arcminutes per pixel
                    pol = "IP", #Specify IP for temperature and E + B Modes, I for temp only, or P for E + B only
                    master_seed = 67, #Specify a seed for reproduceable results
                    r = 0.2, nt = -0.025, k_pivot = 0.002,
                    max_l_tensor = 8_000,
                    max_eta_k_tensor = 16_000,
                    uk_arcmin_t = 3) #Noise level in data fields

We can pick out the fields from the data_set object and then apply the lense_flow() algorithm on them which forward lenses the CMB maps

In [3]: Copied! 
#select the fields from the data_set object
field = data_set.unlensed_field
phi = data_set.phi

#The fields default to Fourier space in the TEB parametrization
#but lense_flow requires converting to Map space in the TQU parametrization
field = map(eb2qu(field))
#The lensing potential has no polarization so we just need to take it to map space
phi = map(phi)

#The first input to lense flow is the field object to be lensed
#and the second input is the lensing potential
lensed_field = lense_flow(field, phi)
#select the fields from the data_set object field = data_set.unlensed_field phi = data_set.phi #The fields default to Fourier space in the TEB parametrization #but lense_flow requires converting to Map space in the TQU parametrization field = map(eb2qu(field)) #The lensing potential has no polarization so we just need to take it to map space phi = map(phi) #The first input to lense flow is the field object to be lensed #and the second input is the lensing potential lensed_field = lense_flow(field, phi)

You can access the underlying data in the fields via the .scalar_matrix, .polar_matrix_1, and .polar_matrix_2 attributes and plot them with standard matplotlib syntax. Here we plot the lensed temperature, polarization fields, and the lensing potential.

We can undo the lensing operation by simply setting the direction = INVERSE_LENSE flag and re-running lense_flow() on the already lensed field to recover the original input field. Behind the scenes, this amounts to just running the ODE solver in reverse.

In [6]: Copied! 
#Inverse lense the fields
lensed_field = map(eb2qu(fourier(lensed_field)))
delensed_field = lense_flow(lensed_field, phi, direction = INVERSE_LENSE)

#Then we can plot the difference between the delensed_field and the original input unlensed field
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize = (16, 8))
im = axes[0].imshow(delensed_field.scalar_matrix - field.scalar_matrix, cmap = "coolwarm")
fig.colorbar(im, ax = axes[0], shrink = 0.5)

plt.show()

In order to converge on accurately estimated lensing potentials and CMB fields, we need an objective function to minimize. The CMBLensing.py package does this by taking gradients of the logpdf function which takes the following mathematical form:

\[-2*\mathrm{logpdf} = \frac{(\mathrm{data} - M * B * L * f)^2}{C_n} + \frac{f^2}{C_f} + \frac{\phi^2}{C_{\phi}}\] \[ + \mathrm{logdet}(C_{\phi}) + \mathrm{logdet}(C_f) + \mathrm{logdet}(C_n)\]

We begin by simulating a data map at the fiducial LCDM cosmology: a single \(64 \times 64\) pixel temperature map with a resolution of \(\theta_\mathrm{pix} = 2.5\) arcminutes per pixel and a noise level of \(5\,\mu\)K-arcmin. The lmax argument sets the maximum multipole CAMB is run to. Beyond it, the power spectra are extrapolated in log space.

In [2]: Copied!

ground_truth_params = load_sim_cosmology(GROUND_TRUTH)
noise_level = 5

Next we run sample_joint, which takes the data set as input and returns samples of the cosmological parameters. Here we sample only \(\ln(10^{10} A_s)\) and hold the other four parameters at their fiducial values, but should_sample can switch on any subset of the five to sample them jointly. In general, the more parameters are sampled jointly, the stronger the degeneracies between them become, and larger maps with finer resolution are needed to obtain meaningful constraints. The chain starts at the lower edge of the search range, far from the ground truth, so that the burn-in is easy to see.

The first time you run the following cell, the ~7.9 GB camb_grid_spline.npz file is downloaded automatically from Hugging Face into the camb_splines/ directory (see Installation), so expect a wait. The two progress plots are written to cmb_lensing/sample_lcdm_output/, which must exist before the cell is run.

With the samples in hand, the next step is to analyze them. The first plot below is the progress plot that sample_joint writes: the trace of the \(\ln(10^{10} A_s)\) samples minus the ground truth value, in units of the parameter's PARAM_SIGMA. There is an initial burn-in because the chain starts far away from the typical set. From around iteration 200 the chain samples from the posterior of \(\ln(10^{10} A_s)\), and the normalized samples scatter within about one sigma of the ground truth.

The second plot is the log-probability of the distribution being sampled. It plateaus even sooner than the parameter trace does, which indicates that the samples of the unlensed field and the lensing potential have a much larger influence on the log-probability than the value of \(\ln(10^{10} A_s)\) does.

The story is essentially the same: the chain starts far from the ground truth, burns in, and then samples from the posterior of \(\ln(10^{10} A_s)\). Below we plot the autocorrelation function against lag, which tells us how correlated two samples are when they are a given number of iterations apart. Summing the autocorrelation function gives a single number, the integrated autocorrelation time (IAT): roughly how many iterations separate two independent samples. Here it turns out to be very small, only about 4. The two functions defined in the cell are also available as autocorrelation and integrated_autocorrelation_time in cmb_lensing/mcmc_diagnostics.py.

#-------- Autocorrelation Function ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
def autocorrelation(chain, max_lag = None):
    """Normalized autocorrelation of a 1D chain of samples."""
    n = len(chain)
    if max_lag is None:
        max_lag = n // 2
    x = chain - np.mean(chain)
    variance = np.var(chain)
    acf = np.correlate(x, x, mode = "full")[n - 1:]  #positive lags only
    acf = acf[:max_lag] / (variance * n)
    return acf

#-------- Integrated Autocorrelation Time -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
def integrated_autocorrelation_time(acf, c = 5.0):
    """Sokal's automatic windowing — truncate at lag M where M < c * tau(M)."""
    tau = 1.0
    for m in range(1, len(acf)):
        tau += 2.0 * acf[m]
        if m >= c * tau:
            return tau
    return tau

acf = autocorrelation(burnt_samples)
iat = np.ceil(integrated_autocorrelation_time(acf))

Here we have drawn samples of a single parameter from a single chain on a single data map. One chain on one map is not a statistically powerful statement, because of MCMC noise and cosmic variance (especially on such a small map). The standard workflow is to run the sampler on many data map realizations at the ground truth cosmology (of order 10 to 100) and, for each map, several sub-chains (typically 5 to 10) that each start from random values of the LCDM parameters.

The analysis then thins every sub-chain by its integrated autocorrelation time, pools the samples of each map, and summarizes each map by a normal distribution with the mean and standard deviation of its samples. The product of these normal distributions over the maps is a single distribution: the best estimate of the parameter given all of the data. The machinery for runs like this is in get_lcdm_samples/ (see LCDM Sampling on the HPC), and Analyzing Chain Data walks through the analysis.

docs.title: Running a Single LCDM Chain¶
docs.text:
The sample_joint function in cmb_lensing/sample_lcdm.py draws samples of the LCDM parameters from the joint posterior \(P(f, \phi, \theta \mid d)\) using a modified version of the Gibbs sampling algorithm introduced by Millea et al. 2020. Here \(f\) is the unlensed CMB field, \(\phi\) the lensing potential, \(\theta\) the LCDM parameters and \(d\) the data.

Five parameters can be sampled: \(100*\theta_\mathrm{MC}\), \(\ln(10^{10} A_s)\), \(n_s\), \(\Omega_b h^2\) and \(\Omega_c h^2\) (theta_MC_100, logA, ns, ombh2 and omch2 in the code). The optical depth to reionization tau is fixed at 0.05 and the neutrino mass mnu at 0.06 eV. The fiducial values of the sampled parameters, their ±5-sigma search ranges and their one-sigma scales are stored as GROUND_TRUTH, PARAM_BOUNDS and PARAM_SIGMA in cmb_lensing/constants.py.

docs.title: One Gibbs iteration¶
docs.text:
The Python implementation mirrors CMBLensing.jl's sample_joint. Each iteration consists of six steps:

  1. \(f\) step (gibbs_sample_f): draw \(f\) from its conditional distribution, as a simulated realization plus a Wiener-filter correction.
  2. mix: change to the mixed parametrization \(f^\circ = L(\phi) \cdot D \cdot f\), \(\phi^\circ = G \cdot \phi\).
  3. \(\phi\) step (gibbs_sample_phi): take one HMC step on the mixed lensing potential \(\phi^\circ\), with the mass matrix \(G^{-2}(C_\phi^{-1} + N_\phi^{-1})\).
  4. \(\theta\) step: for each sampled parameter, make a Gaussian random-walk Metropolis move of width proposal_sigmas[name] on the mixed log-posterior. Proposals outside param_ranges[name] or outside the CAMB grid are rejected.
  5. update \(C_\phi\), \(C_f\), \(D\) and \(G\) at the accepted \(\theta\).
  6. unmix back to \((f, \phi)\) with the updated \(D\) and \(G\).

The \(\theta\) step is skipped for the first num_burn_in_fix_theta iterations.

docs.title: Outputs¶
docs.text: sample_joint returns (param_vals, phi, sub_key): a dictionary holding one list of samples per parameter, the final lensing potential and the final random key. When hpc_path is set, every iteration also appends the latest value of each sampled parameter to {hpc_path}{theta}_map_{map_idx}_chain_{sub_chain_idx}_history.txt. These history files are what cmb_lensing/chain_analysis.py reads (see Analyzing Chain Data).

docs.title: Tuning¶
docs.text:
Before a large experiment, run a pilot chain on a small map (python -m cmb_lensing.sample_lcdm runs one) and tune

  • proposal_sigmas toward an acceptance rate of about 44% per parameter,
  • hmc_step_size and hmc_num_steps toward an acceptance rate of about 65% for \(\phi\).

advanced_logging = {"phi_acceptance": True, "lcdm_acceptance": True, ...} prints the running acceptance rates, and plot_log_pdf / plot_lcdm_sigmas write the progress plots shown above.

def load_chains(chain_dir, burn_in = DEFAULT_BURN_IN):
    """Read every post-burn-in sub-chain in a directory of sample_joint history files.

    A sub-chain is kept when every parameter has its file. Its files are cut to their common
    length (they differ by a sweep when copied from a running job) BEFORE the burn-in is
    removed, so row k of every parameter is the same sweep; a sub-chain no longer than the
    burn-in is left out, and so is a map with no sub-chain left.

    Args:
        chain_dir: directory holding `<param>_map_<seed>_chain_<index>_history.txt` files
        burn_in:   sweeps removed from the start of every sub-chain

    Returns:
        chains (dict): `chains[param][map][sub_chain]` is a 1D array for every GROUND_TRUTH
            parameter with files, in GROUND_TRUTH's order, with maps and sub-chains in the
            same order for every parameter.
        map_seeds (list): the seeds of the kept maps.
    """
    files = find_history_files(chain_dir)
    #every sampled parameter, in GROUND_TRUTH's (= PARAM_ORDER's) order
    params = [name for name in GROUND_TRUTH if name in files]
    shared_keys = sorted(set.intersection(*[set(files[name]) for name in params]))

    chains = {name: [] for name in params}
    map_seeds = []
    num_discarded = 0
    for map_seed in sorted({key[0] for key in shared_keys}):
        sub_chains = {name: [] for name in params}
        for key in [key for key in shared_keys if key[0] == map_seed]:
            histories = [np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(files[name][key])) for name in params]
            common_length = min(len(history) for history in histories)
            if common_length <= burn_in:
                num_discarded += 1
                continue
            for name, history in zip(params, histories):
                sub_chains[name].append(history[burn_in:common_length])
        if len(sub_chains[params[0]]) > 0:
            map_seeds.append(map_seed)
            for name in params:
                chains[name].append(sub_chains[name])
    print(f"Loaded {sum(len(sub_chains) for sub_chains in chains[params[0]])} sub-chains of "
          f"{len(map_seeds)} maps for {params}; discarded {num_discarded} no longer than the "
          f"burn-in of {burn_in}")
    return chains, map_seeds

def get_avg_covariance_matrix(chains):
    """Map-averaged posterior covariance of the sampled parameters, with its jackknife error.

    `chains` is load_chains' dict, whose sub-chains line up row by row across parameters.
    Each map's sub-chains are concatenated and give one covariance matrix, and those are
    averaged over maps. Samples from different maps are never pooled: each map is a
    different data realization with its own posterior mean, so pooling would add the scatter
    of those means to the diagonal. The average is a single-realization posterior, which is
    what a Fisher forecast predicts.

    Returns:
        avg_cov_mat (numpy.ndarray): the per-map covariance matrix averaged over maps.
        param_names (list): the parameters of its rows and columns.
        cov_err (numpy.ndarray): the element-wise error of the averaged covariance, from
            measured_errors.
        sigma_err (numpy.ndarray): the error of each width sqrt(C_ii), from measured_errors.
    """
    param_names = list(chains.keys())
    num_maps = len(chains[param_names[0]])
    per_map_cov_mats = []
    for map_idx in range(num_maps):
        columns = [np.concatenate(chains[name][map_idx]) for name in param_names]
        per_map_cov_mats.append(np.atleast_2d(np.cov(np.column_stack(columns), rowvar = False)))
    per_map_cov_mats = np.array(per_map_cov_mats)
    cov_err, sigma_err = measured_errors(per_map_cov_mats)
    return np.mean(per_map_cov_mats, axis = 0), param_names, cov_err, sigma_err

def get_forecasted_covariance(nside, theta_pix, noise, param_names, delensed_covariance,
                              pol = DEFAULT_POL, qe_filter = DEFAULT_QE_FILTER,
                              phi_noise = None, include_bb = True, ground_truth = GROUND_TRUTH,
                              camb_lmax = CAMB_LMAX):
    """Fisher-forecast covariance of the sampled parameters, with white noise and no beam.

    A thin wrapper of fisher_forecast.forecast. Its field blocks are the empirical delensed
    covariance of `delensed_covariance` (plus the analytic noise); its phi block's noise is
    the box QE N0 or a measured matrix. Build the delensed covariance's Wiener filter from
    the same N_phi.

    Args:
        nside:               pixels per side of the chains' box
        theta_pix:           pixel width in arcmin
        noise:               noise level in uK-arcmin
        param_names:         the sampled parameters; the others are held fixed
        delensed_covariance: a merged delensed_covariance.npz at this box, noise level and
                             `pol` (required)
        pol:                 "I", "P" or "IP": the data the chains saw
        qe_filter:           "unlensed" (default) or "lensed": the spectra in the QE N0's
                             filter. The response always uses the unlensed spectra
        phi_noise:           a merged map_joint_phi_noise.npz / sampler_phi_noise.npz; its
                             `nphi` then replaces the QE N0
        include_bb:          for "P" / "IP", whether the delensed BB block is counted
        ground_truth:        {param_name: value}, the fiducial point, all five parameters
        camb_lmax:           how far CAMB is run

    Returns:
        covariance (numpy.ndarray): the covariance matrix F^-1 over param_names, rows and
            columns in constants.PARAM_ORDER (the order load_chains returns its parameters
            in).
    """
    is_sampled = {name: name in param_names for name in ground_truth}
    fisher, names = forecast(nside, theta_pix, noise, is_sampled, ground_truth,
                             delensed_covariance, pol = pol, qe_filter = qe_filter,
                             phi_noise = phi_noise, include_bb = include_bb,
                             camb_lmax = camb_lmax)
    return covariance_from_fisher(fisher, names)

class DiagonalScalar(FieldOperator):
    """An operator diagonal in Fourier space acting on `FlatS0` fields (e.g. C_TT, C_phi).

    `operator * field` multiplies mode by mode. Operators also combine with each other and
    with scalars through +, - and *; `pinv` and `log_det` are defined for them.

    Attributes:
        scalar_matrix: The diagonal, an (nside, nside//2+1) array on the rfft2 grid.
        nside: Number of pixels on a side.
        theta_pix: Pixel width in arcmin.
        pix_width: Pixel width in radians.
        fourier_weights: Weight of each rfft2 mode.

    #NOTE we must define operator-operator, operator-field, and operator scalar multiplication
    def __mul__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, DiagonalScalar):
            return self.replace(scalar_matrix = self.scalar_matrix * other.scalar_matrix)
        elif isinstance(other, FlatS0):
            return other.replace(scalar_matrix = self.scalar_matrix * other.scalar_matrix)
        else:
            return self.replace(scalar_matrix = self.scalar_matrix * other)

    def __rmul__(self, other):
        return self.__mul__(other)

@struct.dataclass
class BlockTEB(FieldOperator):
    """An operator acting on `FlatS02` fields: per Fourier mode a 2 x 2 T/E block plus an
    independent B block.

    Products with another `BlockTEB` are matrix products of the T/E blocks, so they do not
    commute. `pinv` and `log_det` use Schur complements.

    Attributes:
        matrix_TT: TT block, an (nside, nside//2+1) array on the rfft2 grid.
        matrix_TE: TE block.
        matrix_ET: ET block.
        matrix_EE: EE block.
        matrix_BB: BB block.
        nside: Number of pixels on a side.
        theta_pix: Pixel width in arcmin.
        pix_width: Pixel width in radians.
        fourier_weights: Weight of each rfft2 mode.
    """

    #NOTE these matrices have the following 3 x 3 block diagonal format
    #[TT TE 0 ]
    #[ET EE 0 ]
    #[0  0  BB]

    matrix_TT: jnp.ndarray = flax.struct.field(default_factory = lambda: FOURIER_MATRIX_DEFAULT.copy())
    matrix_TE: jnp.ndarray = flax.struct.field(default_factory = lambda: FOURIER_MATRIX_DEFAULT.copy())
    matrix_ET: jnp.ndarray = flax.struct.field(default_factory = lambda: FOURIER_MATRIX_DEFAULT.copy())
    matrix_EE: jnp.ndarray = flax.struct.field(default_factory = lambda: FOURIER_MATRIX_DEFAULT.copy())
    matrix_BB: jnp.ndarray = flax.struct.field(default_factory = lambda: FOURIER_MATRIX_DEFAULT.copy())

    def _matrix_names(self):
        return {"matrix_TT", "matrix_TE", "matrix_ET", "matrix_EE", "matrix_BB"}

    #NOTE non-diagonal matrix multiplication is NOT commutative hence we need distinction
    #between multiplying on the left or right for BlockTEB matrices specifically
    def __mul__(self, other):

        #matrix-matrix multiplication, matrix-field multiplication, and matrix-scalar multiplication                                                                                                                                                               
        if isinstance(other, BlockTEB):
            #compute a non-diagonal matrix-matrix product                   
            return self.replace(matrix_TT = self.matrix_TT * other.matrix_TT + self.matrix_TE * other.matrix_ET,
                                matrix_ET = self.matrix_ET * other.matrix_TT + self.matrix_EE * other.matrix_ET,
                                matrix_TE = self.matrix_TT * other.matrix_TE + self.matrix_TE * other.matrix_EE,
                                matrix_EE = self.matrix_ET * other.matrix_TE + self.matrix_EE * other.matrix_EE,
                                matrix_BB = self.matrix_BB * other.matrix_BB)
        #matrix-field multiplication
        elif isinstance(other, FlatS02):
            return other.replace(scalar_matrix = self.matrix_TT * other.scalar_matrix + self.matrix_TE * other.polar_matrix_1,
                                 polar_matrix_1 = self.matrix_ET * other.scalar_matrix + self.matrix_EE * other.polar_matrix_1,
                                 polar_matrix_2 = self.matrix_BB * other.polar_matrix_2)
        #matrix-scalar multiplication
        return self.replace(matrix_TT = self.matrix_TT * other,
                            matrix_TE = self.matrix_TE * other,
                            matrix_ET = self.matrix_ET * other,
                            matrix_EE = self.matrix_EE * other,
                            matrix_BB = self.matrix_BB * other)                                                                                                                                         

    #NOTE we only expect to multiply a BlockTEB on the right by another BlockTEB or a scalar
    def __rmul__(self, other): 

        if isinstance(other, BlockTEB):
            #compute a non-diagonal matrix-matrix product                   
            return self.replace(matrix_TT = other.matrix_TT * self.matrix_TT + other.matrix_TE * self.matrix_ET,
                                matrix_ET = other.matrix_ET * self.matrix_TT + other.matrix_EE * self.matrix_ET,
                                matrix_TE = other.matrix_TT * self.matrix_TE + other.matrix_TE * self.matrix_EE,
                                matrix_EE = other.matrix_ET * self.matrix_TE + other.matrix_EE * self.matrix_EE,
                                matrix_BB = other.matrix_BB * self.matrix_BB)
        #matrix-scalar multiplication
        return self.replace(matrix_TT = self.matrix_TT * other,
                            matrix_TE = self.matrix_TE * other,
                            matrix_ET = self.matrix_ET * other,
                            matrix_EE = self.matrix_EE * other,
                            matrix_BB = self.matrix_BB * other)

docs.title: Fisher Forecast
docs.text:
A Gaussian Fisher forecast of the sampler's posterior widths, for temperature (I), polarization (P) or joint (IP) data, from per-mode covariance blocks on the sampler's own rfft grid:

\[ F_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_\text{blocks} \sum_k w_k \, \mathrm{Tr}\!\left[ C_k^{-1} \frac{\partial C_k}{\partial \theta_i}\, C_k^{-1} \frac{\partial C_k}{\partial \theta_j} \right], \]

with \(w_k\) the rfft mode weights (2 per bulk mode, 1 on the self-conjugate columns). For a single-number block the trace is \(\partial_i \ln C_k \, \partial_j \ln C_k\).

Analyzing Chain Data compares the forecast with a set of chains.

docs.title: The blocks
docs.text:
pol Field blocks Phi block I \(C_{TT} + N_{TT}\) \(C_\phi + N_\phi\) P \(C_{EE} + N_{EE}\); \(C_{BB} + N_{BB}\) same IP \(\begin{pmatrix} C_{TT} + N_{TT} & C_{TE} \\ C_{TE} & C_{EE} + N_{EE} \end{pmatrix}\); \(C_{BB} + N_{BB}\) same
  • The field blocks are always measured. Their signal at \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_0 \pm h_i\) is the empirical delensed covariance given as delensed_covariance, measured at the same box, noise level and pol. The finite-difference steps \(h_i\) come from that file. Without the file the forecast is an error: there is no analytic delensing.
  • The noise is analytic and independent of the cosmology, with \(N_{EE} = N_{BB} = 2 N_{TT}\).
  • The phi block uses \(C_\phi(\theta)\) from direct CAMB calls and an \(N_\phi\) held at \(\theta_0\).

docs.title: Choosing N_phi
docs.text:
Option N_phi default the quadratic-estimate \(N^{(0)}\) of the box, built like load_sim's (the TT estimator for I, the EB estimator for P and IP), with the unlensed spectra in both its response and its filter qe_filter = "lensed" (--qe_filter lensed) the same, with the lensed spectra in the filter; the response stays unlensed phi_noise = <npz> (--phi_noise <npz>) the nphi of a merged map_joint_phi_noise.npz or sampler_phi_noise.npz; unmeasured (NaN) modes carry no phi information

Build the delensed covariance's Wiener filter from the same N_phi the forecast uses; nothing checks it.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
python -m cmb_lensing.fisher_forecast --noise 5 --delensed_covariance delensed_covariance.npz
python -m cmb_lensing.fisher_forecast --noise 5 --delensed_covariance delensed_covariance.npz --qe_filter lensed
python -m cmb_lensing.fisher_forecast --noise 5 --delensed_covariance delensed_covariance.npz --phi_noise map_joint_phi_noise.npz
python -m cmb_lensing.fisher_forecast --noise 5 --pol IP --delensed_covariance delensed_covariance_IP.npz
python -m cmb_lensing.fisher_forecast --noise 5 --pol IP --delensed_covariance delensed_covariance_IP.npz --no_bb

Other flags: --nside, --theta_pix, --l_knee, --beam_fwhm, --params (default logA omch2 theta_MC_100), --camb_lmax (default 4000, the support of the simulations).

Outputs go to cmb_lensing/fisher_output/ as fisher_matrix, covariance_matrix, correlation_matrix (PNG) and fisher (npz), each tagged _<pol>_<nphi>_<noise>_uk, e.g. fisher_I_qe_unlensed_5_uk.npz. Parameters are in the package's standard order: theta_MC_100, logA, ns, ombh2, omch2.

docs.title: What the forecast leaves out
docs.text:
• The blocks are added as independent. The residual lensing left in the delensed field tracks \(C_\phi(\theta)\), so the field blocks count some of the lensing information the phi block already has.
  • The delensed BB is pure residual lensing at \(r = 0\). Its modes are neither Gaussian nor independent, so counting them as such is optimistic; include_bb = False (--no_bb) leaves the BB block out and shows how much of a P or IP forecast rests on it.
  • The correlations between the fields and phi are ignored.
  • For IP the \(N^{(0)}\) is the EB estimator's, as in the sampler; a combined temperature and polarization estimator would be lower.
  • Parameters that are not sampled (not in --params) are held fixed, not marginalized over.

def map_joint(data_set, num_steps = 30, constant_step = False):
    """Joint maximum a posteriori estimate of the unlensed field f and the lensing potential phi.

    Alternates a Wiener-filter step for f at the current phi with a step in phi along the
    preconditioned gradient of the mixed logpdf, the step length set by a BFGS line search.
    Starts from f = phi = 0. The cosmology is the one stored in the data set's covariances.

    Args:
        data_set: A `DataSetT`, `DataSetEB` or `DataSetTEB`, e.g. from `load_sim`.
        num_steps: Number of (f step, phi step) iterations.
        constant_step: If True, skip the line search and take unit-length phi steps.

    Returns:
        f (FlatS0 | FlatS2 | FlatS02): the estimated unlensed field, of the same type as
            `data_set.data`, in Fourier space.
        phi (FlatS0): the estimated lensing potential, in Fourier space.

    Example:
        ```python
        from cmb_lensing.simulate import load_sim
        from cmb_lensing.map_joint import map_joint
        data_set = load_sim(nside = 64, theta_pix = 5, pol = "I", master_seed = 1)
        f_map, phi_map = map_joint(data_set)
        ```
    """

    #unpack the necessary data from the data set object
    noise_covariance = data_set.noise_covariance
    mixing_d = data_set.mixing_d
    #MAP joint method is invariant to G matrix so set to identity for simplicity here
    mixing_g = get_scalar_identity(mixing_d)
    field_covariance = data_set.field_covariance
    phi_covariance = data_set.phi_covariance
    quadratic_estimate = data_set.quadratic_estimate
    mask = data_set.mask
    beam = data_set.beam
    data = data_set.data

    #set starting guesses for f and phi to all zeros
    field_predict = 0*data #NOTE this is in general a TEB vector
    phi_predict = zero_scalar_field_like(data) #Phi only ever represents one singular field

    #compute the hessian which we will use to calculate the step in the phi direction 
    hessian = pinv(phi_gradient_hessian(phi_covariance, quadratic_estimate))
    alpha = jnp.array(1.0)
    for _ in range(num_steps):

        #compute the wiener filter of the predicted field
        field_predict = wiener_filter(field_predict, phi_predict, data, field_covariance, noise_covariance, mask, beam)

        #must mix f and phi before taking the gradient
        mixed_field, mixed_phi = mix(field_predict, phi_predict, mixing_d, mixing_g)
        mixed_grad_phi = mixed_grad_phi_logpdf(mixed_field, mixed_phi, data, noise_covariance, 
                                                phi_covariance, field_covariance, 
                                                mask, beam, mixing_d, mixing_g)

        #create a new partial function whose only input is alpha for use in the brent optimizer (we want to
        #minimize the value of this function w.r.t. the single parameter alpha)
        min_logpdf = partial(logpdf_at_phi_new, grad_phi = mixed_grad_phi, mixed_field = mixed_field, 
                             phi_predict = mixed_phi, data = data, beam = beam, mask = mask, field_covariance = field_covariance,
                             phi_covariance = phi_covariance, noise_covariance = noise_covariance,
                             mixing_d = mixing_d, mixing_g = mixing_g, hessian = hessian)

        if not constant_step:
            #call the optimizer to find which alpha minimizes the best
            optimizer = minimize(min_logpdf, 1, method = "BFGS") #Set a starting guess of "alpha = 1"
            alpha = optimizer.x[0]

        #take a step in the opposite direction of the gradient
        phi_predict = phi_predict + alpha * hessian * mixed_grad_phi

    #after max iterations have been looped through return the final learned fields
    return field_predict, phi_predict

def sample_joint(data_set, param_init, proposal_sigmas, param_ranges, should_sample, noise_level, 
                 advanced_logging, fixed_fields = False, phi_init = "MAP",
                 hmc_num_steps = DEFAULT_HMC_NUM_STEPS, hmc_step_size = DEFAULT_HMC_STEP_SIZE,
                 iters_per_chain = 10_000, num_burn_in_fix_theta = 100, num_burn_in_always_accept = 0, 
                 resume_chain_dict = None, seed = None, map_idx = 1, sub_chain_idx = 1,
                 lmax = DEFAULT_MAX_ELL, metropolis_num_steps = 1, hpc_path = None):
    """Gibbs-sample the joint posterior P(f, phi, theta | d) of the field, the lensing potential
    and the five LCDM parameters.

    Each iteration draws f from its conditional, takes one HMC step on the mixed phi, then one
    random-walk Metropolis move per sampled parameter on the mixed logpdf, and recomputes the
    covariance and mixing matrices at the accepted parameters. The parameters are named as in
    `constants.PARAM_ORDER`: "theta_MC_100", "logA", "ns", "ombh2", "omch2". The spectra come
    from the 5D CAMB grid spline (`camb_splines/camb_grid_spline.npz`, downloaded on first
    use).

    Args:
        data_set: The data, a `DataSetT`, `DataSetEB` or `DataSetTEB` (e.g. from
            `load_sim`). Its type sets the polarization mode.
        param_init: {name: value} starting point, all five parameters.
        proposal_sigmas: {name: width} of the Gaussian Metropolis proposal per parameter.
            The parameters are updated in this dict's order. Tune toward ~44 % acceptance.
        param_ranges: {name: (low, high)}; proposals outside the range are rejected.
        should_sample: {name: bool}; parameters set to False stay at `param_init`.
        noise_level: White noise level of the data in uK-arcmin.
        advanced_logging: {"phi_acceptance", "lcdm_acceptance", "plot_log_pdf",
            "plot_lcdm_sigmas": bool}. The first two print running acceptance rates, the
            last two overwrite progress plots in `cmb_lensing/sample_lcdm_output/` (which
            must exist) every iteration.
        fixed_fields: Debugging option: hold f and phi at the data set's true fields and
            sample theta only.
        phi_init: Starting phi: "MAP" (the `map_joint` estimate, default), "RNG" (a draw
            from the phi step's inverse mass matrix) or anything else for zero.
        hmc_num_steps: Leapfrog steps per phi HMC step.
        hmc_step_size: Leapfrog step size. Tune toward ~65 % phi acceptance.
        iters_per_chain: Number of Gibbs iterations.
        num_burn_in_fix_theta: Iterations before the parameters start to move.
        num_burn_in_always_accept: Iterations for which every phi HMC step is accepted.
        resume_chain_dict: Restart a saved chain: a dict with one entry per parameter name,
            "phi_map" and "sub_key" (e.g. `np.load` of the npz `run_single_lcdm_chain.py`
            writes). Overrides `param_init` and `phi_init`.
        seed: Seed of the chain's random numbers. None draws one at random.
        map_idx: Data-map index used in the history file names.
        sub_chain_idx: Chain index used in the history file names.
        lmax: Largest multipole of the spectra.
        metropolis_num_steps: Metropolis moves per parameter per iteration.
        hpc_path: If set, every iteration appends each sampled parameter's latest value to
            `{hpc_path}{name}_map_{map_idx}_chain_{sub_chain_idx}_history.txt`.

    Returns:
        param_vals (dict): per parameter name, the list of the chain's values, starting
            with `param_init`.
        phi (FlatS0): the final lensing potential.
        sub_key (jax.Array): the final random key. Together with `phi` and the last
            parameter values it lets a chain be resumed.
    """

    #polarization mode follows the dataset
    if isinstance(data_set, DataSetTEB):
        pol = "IP"
    elif isinstance(data_set, DataSetEB):
        pol = "P"
    elif isinstance(data_set, DataSetT):
        pol = "I"
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"sample_joint supports DataSetT (pol = 'I'), DataSetEB "
                         f"(pol = 'P') and DataSetTEB (pol = 'IP') datasets, got "
                         f"{type(data_set).__name__}")
    bb_is_zero = camb_grid_bb_is_zero()

    #if a resume_chain_dict is specified (e.g. np.load of the npz run_single_lcdm_chain.py
    #writes: one entry per parameter name, "phi_map" and "sub_key"), restart from its parameters
    if resume_chain_dict is not None:
        param_init = {}
        for name in PARAM_ORDER:
            param_init[name] = float(resume_chain_dict[name])

    #the sampled parameters, in PARAM_ORDER: the ones whose histories are logged
    theta_log_names = [name for name in PARAM_ORDER if should_sample.get(name, False)]

    #the 5D grid predictors, checked at the starting point before anything heavy runs
    predictors = get_camb_grid_predictors()
    start_tt = predictors.tt(jnp.array([[param_init[k] for k in PARAM_ORDER]]))
    if not bool(jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(start_tt))):
        raise ValueError(
            f"the starting parameters {dict((k, param_init[k]) for k in PARAM_ORDER)} "
            f"fall outside the 5D CAMB grid, so the initial covariances would be NaN. "
            f"Check that theta_MC_100 is reachable at this ombh2/omch2 - see "
            f"theta_grid in {CAMB_GRID_PATH}")

    #Set the initial parameter values to the user specified starting guesses
    param_vals = {}
    for theta, theta_val in param_init.items():
        param_vals[theta] = [theta_val]
    #Also store the current parameter values in a JAX array
    current_params = jnp.array([param_init[k] for k in PARAM_ORDER], dtype = jnp.float64)

    #Add data that will be used throughout the sampling algorithm to an args dictionary
    args = {}
    args = add_metadata_to_args(args, data_set, lmax)
    args = add_starting_matrices_to_args(args, data_set, noise_level,
                                         param_init, current_params,
                                         predictors, pol = pol)

    #change data_set covariance matrices from ground truth to initial
    #starting point in cosmological parameter space
    data_set = set_initial_ds_conditions(data_set, args)
    data_field = data_set.data

    #Use a seed to get reproduceable results if so desired
    #otherwise use machine entropy to generate a random number
    if seed is not None:
        sub_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed)
    elif resume_chain_dict is not None:
        sub_key = jnp.asarray(resume_chain_dict["sub_key"])
    else:
        sub_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(np.random.randint(0, 2**31))

    #Setting the starting point in phi-space to be the MAP estimate (the mode) plus a random realization
    #of the Hessian pre-conditioner empirically seems to decrease the burn-in time (DEFAULT).
    #A resumed chain starts from its saved phi whatever phi_init says
    if resume_chain_dict is not None:
        phi = data_set.phi.replace(scalar_matrix = jnp.asarray(resume_chain_dict["phi_map"]))
    elif phi_init == "MAP":
        _, phi_map = map_joint(data_set)
        phi = phi_map
    elif phi_init == "RNG":
        inv_mass_matrix = pinv(pinv(args["phi_covariance"]) + pinv(args["quadratic_estimate"]))
        rng_key, sub_key = jax.random.split(sub_key)
        phi_rng_matrix = field_from_covar_single_key(data_set.data.nside, inv_mass_matrix.scalar_matrix, rng_key)
        phi = data_set.phi.replace(scalar_matrix = jfft.rfft2(phi_rng_matrix))
    else:
        phi = 0*data_set.phi

    #We repeatedly draw a fresh temperature / polarization field, so we need a "zeroes" object
    #of the same class as the temperature / polarization field
    field_zeroes = 0*data_set.unlensed_field

    #the stacked data matrices handed to every jitted theta kernel
    data_stack = field_matrix_stack(data_field, pol)

    #lists used to track sampling acceptance rates
    phi_acceptance = []
    mixed_logpdf_values = []
    lcdm_acceptance = {}
    lcdm_acceptance["theta_MC_100"] = []
    lcdm_acceptance["ombh2"] = []
    lcdm_acceptance["omch2"] = []
    lcdm_acceptance["ns"] = []
    lcdm_acceptance["logA"] = []

    for iter in range(1, iters_per_chain + 1):

        #The "fixed_fields" flag can be used for quick debugging of the theta step 
        #assuming we have perfect knowledge of the ground truth (f, phi) pair
        if not fixed_fields:
            #1. sample the temperature field
            rng_key, sub_key = jax.random.split(sub_key)
            temp_field = gibbs_sample_f(field_zeroes, data_field, phi, args, rng_key)

            #2. mix the fields
            mixed_temp, mixed_phi = mix(temp_field, phi, args["mixing_d"], args["mixing_g"])

            #3. sample the lensing potential phi
            rng_key, sub_key = jax.random.split(sub_key)
            mixed_phi, delta_h, accept = gibbs_sample_phi(mixed_phi, mixed_temp, data_field, rng_key,
                                                          args, iter, num_burn_in_always_accept,
                                                          hmc_num_steps = hmc_num_steps, 
                                                          hmc_step_size = hmc_step_size)
            if advanced_logging["phi_acceptance"]:
                phi_acceptance.append(int(accept))
                print(f"Phi accept rate = {np.sum(np.array(phi_acceptance)) / len(phi_acceptance)}")
                print(f"delta_H = {delta_h}")
        else:
            mixed_temp, mixed_phi = mix(data_set.unlensed_field, data_set.phi, 
                                        args["mixing_d"], args["mixing_g"])

        #4. sample your cosmo parameters
        if iter >= num_burn_in_fix_theta:
            for theta, proposal_sigma in list(proposal_sigmas.items()):
                if should_sample[theta]:
                    rng_key, sub_key = jax.random.split(sub_key)
                    theta_key_idx = PARAM_INDEX[theta]
                    theta_val = gibbs_sample_theta(jnp.array(theta_key_idx), param_ranges[theta], 
                                                   jnp.array(param_vals[theta][-1]),
                                                   lcdm_acceptance, advanced_logging["lcdm_acceptance"],
                                                   field_matrix_stack(mixed_temp, pol),
                                                   mixed_phi.scalar_matrix, data_stack,
                                                   current_params, rng_key, 
                                                   args["nside"], args["pix_width"], data_field.theta_pix,
                                                   args["ell_grid"],
                                                   args["quadratic_estimate"].scalar_matrix,
                                                   op_matrix_stack(args["noise_covariance"], pol),
                                                   op_shared_matrix(args["mask"], pol), 
                                                   op_shared_matrix(args["beam"], pol),
                                                   data_field.fourier_weights,
                                                   proposal_sigma = proposal_sigma,
                                                   metropolis_num_steps = metropolis_num_steps,
                                                   pol = pol, bb_is_zero = bb_is_zero)
                    param_vals[theta].append(theta_val)
                    current_params = current_params.at[theta_key_idx].set(theta_val)

            #5. recompute mixing and covariance matrices using the newly sampled parameter values
            args = update_args_after_sample(current_params, predictors, args, pol = pol)

        #6. unmix the fields using the updated version of the G & D matrices
        if not fixed_fields:
            _, phi = unmix(mixed_temp, mixed_phi, args["mixing_d"], args["mixing_g"])

        #7. plot certain diagnostics if user specified
        if advanced_logging["plot_log_pdf"]:
            mixed_logpdf_value = mixed_logpdf(mixed_temp, mixed_phi, data_field, args["noise_covariance"], 
                                              args["phi_covariance"], args["field_covariance"], 
                                              args["mask"], args["beam"], 
                                              args["mixing_g"], args["mixing_d"])
            mixed_logpdf_values.append(mixed_logpdf_value)
            plt.figure(figsize = (16, 10))
            plt.plot(mixed_logpdf_values, marker = "o")
            plt.title("Mixed LogPDF Over Time")
            plt.xlabel("Iteration")
            plt.ylabel("Mixed LogPDF Value")
            plt.legend()
            path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))),
                                "cmb_lensing", "sample_lcdm_output", "logpdf_progress.png")
            plt.savefig(path)
            plt.close() 

        if advanced_logging["plot_lcdm_sigmas"]:
            plt.figure(figsize = (16, 10))
            for name in theta_log_names:
                normalized = (np.array(param_vals[name]) - GROUND_TRUTH[name]) / PARAM_SIGMA[name]
                plt.plot(normalized, label = name, marker = "o")
            plt.axhline(0, color = "black", label = "Zero Sigma")
            plt.axhline(1, color = "grey", label = "+/- 1 Sigma")
            plt.axhline(-1, color = "grey")
            plt.title("(mean - sample)/sigma")
            plt.xlabel("Iteration")
            plt.ylabel("Standard Deviations")
            plt.legend()
            path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))),
                                "cmb_lensing", "sample_lcdm_output", "lcdm_progress.png")
            plt.savefig(path)
            plt.close()

        #Log chains to .txt files if we are running a larger experiment on an HPC
        if hpc_path is not None:
            for theta in theta_log_names:
                theta_path = hpc_path + f"{theta}_map_{map_idx}_chain_{sub_chain_idx}_history.txt"
                with open(theta_path, "a") as file:
                    file.write(str(param_vals[theta][-1]) + "\n")

    return param_vals, phi, sub_key

def load_sim(nside, theta_pix, pol, master_seed, uk_arcmin_t = 3, H0 = None,
             ombh2 = 0.0224567, omch2 = 0.118489, cosmomc_theta = 0.0104098,
             r = 0.0, mnu = DEFAULT_MNU, tau = DEFAULT_TAUREIO, As = jnp.exp(3.043) * 1e-10,
             nt = 0, ns = 0.968602, lmax = 4000, begin_ell_interp = None, l_knee = 100,
             k_pivot = DEFAULT_K_PIVOT, Alens = DEFAULT_A_LENSE, nphi_fac = 2, a_phi = 1,
             precomputed_cls = None, max_l_tensor = DEFAULT_MAX_L_TENSOR,
             max_eta_k_tensor = DEFAULT_MAX_ETA_K_TENSOR, use_mask = False):
    """Simulate a lensed CMB data set on a flat nside x nside sky patch.

    Runs CAMB for the requested cosmology, builds the field, phi and noise covariances in
    Fourier space, draws the unlensed field(s), phi and the noise, lenses the field with
    LenseFlow and returns everything in one data set object. CAMB runs inside
    `jax.pure_callback`, so a CAMB failure gives NaN spectra rather than an exception.

    Randomness: one root key PRNGKey(master_seed), and every random field (phi, then the
    unlensed field(s), then the noise) splits its own subkey off it in that fixed order
    (field_from_covar). So the realization at a seed depends on the cosmology only through
    the covariances the white noise is scaled by.

    Args:
        nside: Number of pixels on a side.
        theta_pix: Pixel width in arcmin.
        pol: "I" (temperature only), "P" (E/B polarization only) or "IP" (both).
        master_seed: Root seed of every random draw.
        uk_arcmin_t: White noise level in temperature, in uK-arcmin. The polarization
            noise is sqrt(2) higher.
        H0: Hubble constant. Leave as None to set the expansion through `cosmomc_theta`.
        ombh2: Physical baryon density.
        omch2: Physical cold dark matter density.
        cosmomc_theta: CosmoMC's approximation to the angular size of the sound horizon
            (the sampler's theta_MC_100 divided by 100).
        r: Tensor-to-scalar ratio.
        mnu: Sum of the neutrino masses in eV.
        tau: Optical depth to reionization.
        As: Primordial scalar amplitude (the sampler's logA is log(1e10 As)).
        nt: Tensor spectral index.
        ns: Scalar spectral index.
        lmax: Largest multipole of the spectra.
        begin_ell_interp: Optional multipole past which the spectra are extrapolated
            rather than taken from CAMB.
        l_knee: Knee of the 1/f noise term. 0 gives pure white noise, as every sampler
            entry point uses.
        k_pivot: Pivot scale of the primordial spectra, in 1/Mpc.
        Alens: CAMB's lensing amplitude.
        nphi_fac: Factor the quadratic-estimate noise is divided by (CMBLensing.jl's
            preconditioning heuristic).
        a_phi: Amplitude multiplying the phi covariance.
        precomputed_cls: Optional dict of CAMB spectra to use instead of running CAMB, for
            callers that build many realizations at one cosmology. It must be in
            `_extract_all_cls`'s format (e.g. the output of
            `fisher_forecast.camb_cls_at_params`) and must belong to the same cosmology as
            the keyword arguments, which are then unused.
        max_l_tensor: CAMB's largest multipole for the tensor spectra.
        max_eta_k_tensor: CAMB's largest k * eta for the tensor spectra.
        use_mask: Apply a sky mask. False (the default) uses a mask of all ones.

    Returns:
        data_set (DataSetT | DataSetEB | DataSetTEB): a `DataSetT` (pol = "I"), `DataSetEB`
            (pol = "P") or `DataSetTEB` (pol = "IP") holding the fields (`unlensed_field`,
            `lensed_field`, `phi`, `data`) and the operators (`field_covariance`,
            `phi_covariance`, `noise_covariance`, `mask`, `beam`, `mixing_d`, `mixing_g`,
            `quadratic_estimate`, ...). All fields are in Fourier space.

    Example:
        ```python
        from cmb_lensing.simulate import load_sim
        data_set = load_sim(nside = 128, theta_pix = 2.5, pol = "IP", master_seed = 67,
                            uk_arcmin_t = 5, l_knee = 0)
        ```
    """

    lmax_prime = min(lmax, DEFAULT_MAX_ELL) if begin_ell_interp is None else min(lmax, begin_ell_interp)

    if precomputed_cls is None:
        unlensed_scalar, tensor, total, lens_potential = _camb_via_callback(
            H0, ombh2, omch2, cosmomc_theta, r, mnu, tau, As, nt, ns,
            lmax_prime, k_pivot, Alens, max_l_tensor, max_eta_k_tensor
        )
        cls = _extract_all_cls(unlensed_scalar, tensor, total, lens_potential, lmax, lmax_prime)
    else:
        cls = _validate_precomputed_cls(precomputed_cls, lmax)

    ell_grid, pix_width = gen_ell_grid(nside, theta_pix)
    #one root key; every draw below splits its own subkey off it (field_from_covar). The draw
    #ORDER (phi, the field(s), the noise) is fixed and independent of the cosmology, so two
    #calls at the same seed share every white-noise realization - the common random numbers
    #delensed_covariance.py's stencil relies on
    #TEMPORARY, REMOVE AFTER TESTING: pre-2026-10-16 RNG keys (reproduces the August 2026
    #maps): one batch of pre-split keys, consumed in order. Restore:
    #    rng_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(master_seed)
    rng_key = (jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(master_seed), LEGACY_NUM_KEYS), 0)
    ells = jnp.arange(2, lmax).astype(jnp.float64)

    #ells arrays matched to the cls lengths: the emulator override returns ells
    #2..lmax inclusive while the CAMB dl2cl path returns 2..lmax-1
    phi_ells = jnp.arange(2, 2 + cls["phi"].shape[0]).astype(jnp.float64)

    #Lensing potential
    unscaled_cphi = covar_matrix_from_cls(nside, pix_width, ell_grid,
                                          phi_ells,
                                          cls["phi"], origin_value=0)
    cphi = a_phi * unscaled_cphi
    phi, rng_key = field_from_covar(nside, cphi, rng_key)

    #Unlensed field covariances (scalar + tensor). Unlensed scalar BB (identically zero
    #at r = 0) cannot go through the log-interpolating covariance builder (log(0) -> NaN)
    #so _covar_or_zeros maps it to an exactly zero matrix. TE crosses zero, so it is
    #built from the correlation ratio rho = Cl_TE / sqrt(Cl_TT * Cl_EE) instead
    #(te_covar_from_rho): linear interpolation of rho onto the ell grid, scaled by
    #sqrt(cf_tt * cf_ee), which keeps the T/E block positive semi-definite by
    #construction and matched to the sampler's grid-spline TE path
    cf = {}
    cf_scalar = {}
    cf_tensor = {}
    pol_comps = ("TT",) if pol == "I" else ("TT", "EE", "BB")
    for comp in pol_comps:
        scalar_ells = jnp.arange(2, 2 + cls[f"scalar_{comp}"].shape[0]).astype(jnp.float64)
        cf_scalar[comp] = _covar_or_zeros(nside, pix_width, ell_grid,
                                          scalar_ells,
                                          cls[f"scalar_{comp}"], origin_value=0)
        cf_tensor[comp] = _covar_or_zeros(nside, pix_width, ell_grid, ells,
                                          cls[f"tensor_{comp}"], origin_value=0)
        cf[comp] = cf_scalar[comp] + cf_tensor[comp]
    if pol != "I":
        scalar_ells = jnp.arange(2, 2 + cls["scalar_TE"].shape[0]).astype(jnp.float64)
        rho_te = te_rho_from_cls(cls["scalar_TE"], cls["scalar_TT"], cls["scalar_EE"])
        cf["TE"] = cf_scalar["TE"] = te_covar_from_rho(rho_te, scalar_ells, ell_grid,
                                                       cf["TT"], cf["EE"])
        cf_tensor["TE"] = jnp.zeros((nside, nside // 2 + 1))

    #Lensed field covariances (TE via the same correlation-ratio route)
    cfl = {comp: covar_matrix_from_cls(nside, pix_width, ell_grid, ells,
                                       cls[f"total_{comp}"], origin_value=0)
           for comp in ("TT", "EE", "BB")}
    rho_te_lensed = te_rho_from_cls(cls["total_TE"], cls["total_TT"], cls["total_EE"])
    cfl["TE"] = te_covar_from_rho(rho_te_lensed, ells, ell_grid, cfl["TT"], cfl["EE"])

    #Unlensed random fields. T and E are drawn CORRELATED to match the model's TE block:
    #E ~ N(0, C_EE), then T = (C_TE / C_EE) E + t_indep with
    #t_indep ~ N(0, C_TT - C_TE^2 / C_EE), which gives exactly
    #Cov = [[C_TT, C_TE], [C_TE, C_EE]] (the conditional variance is
    #C_TT (1 - rho^2) >= 0 by the |rho| <= 1 construction; the maximum(0) guards
    #round-off only). The B draw against a zero covariance gives an exactly zero field
    if pol == "I":
        field_t, rng_key = field_from_covar(nside, cf["TT"], rng_key)
    else:
        conditional_tt = jnp.maximum(
            cf["TT"] - cf["TE"]**2 * reciprocal_matrix(cf["EE"]), 0.0)
        t_indep, rng_key = field_from_covar(nside, conditional_tt, rng_key)
        field_e, rng_key = field_from_covar(nside, cf["EE"], rng_key)
        field_b, rng_key = field_from_covar(nside, cf["BB"], rng_key)
        te_ratio = cf["TE"] * reciprocal_matrix(cf["EE"])
        field_t = jfft.irfft2(te_ratio * jfft.rfft2(field_e)) + t_indep

    #Lensing
    if pol == "I":
        lensed_t = jfft.rfft2(primal_lense_flow(
            field_t, phi, pix_width, n=10, direction=FORWARD_LENSE, adjoint=False
        ))
    else:
        lensed_t, lensed_e, lensed_b = _lens_fields(
            field_t, field_e, field_b, phi, pix_width, nside, theta_pix
        )

    beam = get_beam(nside, pix_width, ell_grid, lmax_prime)
    #NOTE we have removed the mask for LCDM inference
    mask = get_mask(DEFAULT_MASK_ELL, nside, pix_width, ell_grid) if use_mask else jnp.ones_like(beam)

    #Noise covariance and white noise (the TE noise Cls are identically zero, so
    #_covar_or_zeros keeps that block an exact zero matrix instead of NaN)
    n_tt, n_te, n_ee, n_bb = noise_cls(lmax_prime, uk_arcmin_t, l_knee = l_knee)
    ell_prime = jnp.arange(2, lmax_prime)
    cn = {}
    for comp, ncl in zip(("TT", "TE", "EE", "BB"), (n_tt, n_te, n_ee, n_bb)):
        cn[comp] = _covar_or_zeros(nside, pix_width, ell_grid, ell_prime, ncl, origin_value=0)

    wn_t, rng_key = field_from_covar(nside, cn["TT"], rng_key)
    if pol != "I":
        wn_e, rng_key = field_from_covar(nside, cn["EE"], rng_key)
        wn_b, rng_key = field_from_covar(nside, cn["BB"], rng_key)

    #Data = Mask * Beam * Lensed + Noise
    data_t = mask * beam * lensed_t + jfft.rfft2(wn_t)
    if pol != "I":
        data_e = mask * beam * lensed_e + jfft.rfft2(wn_e)
        data_b = mask * beam * lensed_b + jfft.rfft2(wn_b)

    #Convert unlensed fields to Fourier space
    field_t = jfft.rfft2(field_t)
    if pol != "I":
        field_e, field_b = jfft.rfft2(field_e), jfft.rfft2(field_b)

    #D matrix (full T/E block including TE; see get_d_teb_matrix for the identity B
    #block at r = 0)
    d_tt = get_d_tt_matrix(cf["TT"], cn["TT"])
    if pol != "I":
        d_tt, d_te, d_ee, d_bb = get_d_teb_matrix(cf["TT"], cf["TE"], cf["EE"], cf["BB"],
                                                  cn["TT"], cn["TE"], cn["EE"], cn["BB"])

    #Quadratic estimate
    if pol == "I":
        qe = scalar_quadratic_estimate(cn["TT"], cf["TT"], cfl["TT"],
                                       mask, beam, pix_width) / nphi_fac
    else:
        qe = polar_quadratic_estimate(cf["EE"], cf["BB"], cfl["EE"], cfl["BB"],
                                      cn["EE"], cn["BB"], mask, mask,
                                      beam, beam, pix_width) / nphi_fac

    #The G mixing matrix    
    g = get_g_matrix(cphi, qe, a_phi, a_phi = a_phi)

    #convert phi back to fourier space
    phi = jfft.rfft2(phi)
    #Build dataset for the requested polarization
    if pol == "I":
        return _build_dataset_t(
            nside, theta_pix, pix_width, cphi, unscaled_cphi, qe, phi,
            cf, cf_scalar, cf_tensor, cfl, cn, d_tt, g, mask, beam,
            field_t, lensed_t, data_t, r, a_phi
        )
    elif pol == "P":
        return _build_dataset_eb(
            nside, theta_pix, pix_width, cphi, unscaled_cphi, qe, phi,
            cf, cf_scalar, cf_tensor, cfl, cn, d_ee, d_bb, g, mask, beam,
            field_e, field_b, lensed_e, lensed_b, data_e, data_b, r, a_phi
        )
    else:
        return _build_dataset_teb(
            nside, theta_pix, pix_width, cphi, unscaled_cphi, qe, phi,
            cf, cf_scalar, cf_tensor, cfl, cn, d_tt, d_te, d_ee, d_bb, g, mask, beam,
            field_t, field_e, field_b,
            lensed_t, lensed_e, lensed_b,
            data_t, data_e, data_b, r, a_phi
        )

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Maps live on a flat, periodic nside x nside box with theta_pix arcminutes per pixel. Three field types (cmb_lensing/fields.py) cover the polarization modes:

Type Content Arrays FlatS0 a scalar map (e.g. temperature or lensing potential) scalar_matrix FlatS2 polarization (E/B - Modes or Q/U - Modes) polar_matrix_1, polar_matrix_2 FlatS02 temperature + polarization scalar_matrix, polar_matrix_1, polar_matrix_2

A field carries a basis: either MAP (real space, (nside, nside), float64) or FOURIER (the rfft2 half plane, (nside, nside//2 + 1) complex128). Polarization is implicitly in either the EB or the QU parametrization. The conversions are

field = map(field)        #FOURIER -> MAP (irfft2)
field = fourier(field)    #MAP -> FOURIER (rfft2)
field = eb2qu(field)      #EB -> QU (in Fourier)
field = qu2eb(field)      #QU -> EB (in Fourier)

lense_flow takes fields in MAP / QU. Most other code works in FOURIER / EB.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Diagonal-in-Fourier operators (covariances, beam, mask, the mixing matrices) are in cmb_lensing/matrix_operators.py:

Type Used for DiagonalScalar T-only, and every phi operator DiagonalEB E/B operators BlockTEB T/E/B operators with a 2x2 T/E block (TT, TE, ET, EE, BB)

Arithmetic is element-wise per block, except BlockTEB multiplication, which is the 2x2 T/E matrix product. pinv and log_det dispatch on the operator type.

Fields and operators are flax.struct.dataclass pytrees, so they pass through jax.jit, jax.grad and jax.vmap directly.

docs.text:
cmb_lensing.simulate.load_sim is the main entry point. It

  1. runs CAMB for the requested cosmology,
  2. builds the field, phi and noise covariances in Fourier space,
  3. draws the unlensed field, phi and the noise,
  4. lenses the field with primal_lense_flow,
  5. returns a DataSetT / DataSetEB / DataSetTEB holding the fields, the operators and the simulated data.
from cmb_lensing.simulate import load_sim
data_set = load_sim(nside = 128,         #pixels per side
                    theta_pix = 2.5,     #arcmin per pixel
                    pol = "IP",          #"I", "P" or "IP"
                    master_seed = 67,
                    uk_arcmin_t = 5,     #white noise level in T (P is sqrt(2) higher)
                    l_knee = 0)          #0 for pure white noise

Useful attributes of the returned data set: unlensed_field, lensed_field, phi, data, field_covariance, phi_covariance, noise_covariance, mask, beam, mixing_d, mixing_g, quadratic_estimate.

Only the CAMB grid is downloaded automatically (Installation). Fetch anything else with the hf command that huggingface_hub installs, one folder at a time:

docs.title: Developing
docs.text: Bug reports, questions, documentation fixes and code contributions are all welcome. This page explains how to set up a development environment, run the unit tests and propose a change. The same guidelines are in the file CONTRIBUTING.md of the repository.

docs.title: Getting help and reporting a bug
docs.text:
All support goes through GitHub Issues. For a question, say so in the title of the issue (for example "Question: ..."), and search the existing issues first in case it has already been answered.

A bug report should include:

  • what you ran, ideally a short script that reproduces the problem,
  • what you expected to happen and what happened instead, with the full error traceback if there is one,
  • the run configuration: the polarization mode ("I", "P" or "IP"), nside, theta_pix, the noise level, and whether the 5D CAMB grid was the downloaded one or one you rebuilt,
  • your environment: the operating system, the Python version, the versions of jax, jaxlib and camb, and whether you ran on a CPU or a GPU.

For a result that looks wrong rather than a crash, include a plot or the numbers you compared against.

To suggest a feature, open an issue that describes what you would like to do and why. For a larger change, open the issue before writing code, so the approach can be agreed on first.

docs.title: Setting up a development environment
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install it in editable mode, with the extra packages for the tests and the documentation:

git clone https://github.com/zaneblood1/CMBLensing.py.git
cd CMBLensing.py
pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"

The LCDM sampler also needs the 5D CAMB grid, which is downloaded on first use (see Installation). Its folder camb_splines/ is gitignored: never commit or force-add these files.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
Most tests compare CMBLensing.py with CMBLensing.jl: given the same inputs, the Python and Julia outputs should agree to numerical precision. The Julia outputs are stored in the repository, in the folder tests/ground_truth_data/, so the tests run without Julia installed.

The Julia outputs come from commit 8e75a7c of CMBLensing.jl, run with Julia 1.11.

Test file What it checks test_covariance_matrices.py, test_simulated_cls.py the spectra and covariances of the simulation test_lensing.py the lensing operation test_logpdf.py, test_gradients.py the log-probability and its gradients test_wiener_filter.py, test_map_joint.py the Wiener filter and the MAP estimate test_camb_grid.py the 5D CAMB grid against direct CAMB calls (skipped when the grid file is absent)

The LCDM sampler, the Fisher forecast and the noise measurement modules have no tests.

These comparisons are closer to validation benchmarks than to unit tests: they check whole functions against Julia. Each one fails when a regression is introduced that makes the Python and Julia versions differ past a threshold (see When a test fails). Unit tests that check small pieces of the code in isolation are an area for future development and improvement.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
Run every test from the repository root:

pytest

Or run a single file:

pytest tests/test_lensing.py

docs.title: When a test fails
docs.text:
Every comparison measures a difference between the Python and the Julia output and fails when that difference exceeds a threshold. The thresholds are set from the differences measured on 2026-11-24, which each test file lists at its top (MEASURED_NORM_DIFF, MEASURED_DECORRELATION, ...): a comparison may reach REGRESSION_MARGIN (2) times its measured difference before it fails, and comparisons that agree to round-off are allowed ROUND_OFF_TOLERANCE (1e-12). Both constants are in tests/regression_thresholds.py.

A failing test therefore means that a change to the code moved the Python output away from the Julia output. If the change is intended and the new difference is understood, update the measured value in the test file.

The tests also write comparison plots into the folder tests/test_generated_figures/ (the Python and Julia outputs, their difference and their cross correlation). The page tests/index.html displays them; open it through a local server such as the VS Code Live Server extension. Opening it is not necessary, since the tests fail on their own, but the plots can help with debugging when a test fails: they show where on the map, or at which multipoles, the two outputs differ.

docs.title: Regenerating the Julia data
docs.text:
This is only needed when the Julia reference data has to change. It requires Julia, a CMBLensing.jl checkout at the commit above, and the Python package juliacall.

Step 1. Install juliacall into your Python environment.

pip install juliacall

Step 2. Make Julia 1.11 your default version. The commands below use juliaup.

juliaup add 1.11
juliaup default 1.11
julia --version

The last command should print a 1.11 version, for example:

julia version 1.11.9

Step 3. Clone CMBLensing.jl and check out the commit. A clone always fetches the latest version, so the commit is checked out afterwards.

git clone https://github.com/marius311/CMBLensing.jl.git
cd CMBLensing.jl
git checkout 8e75a7c56e37d337256c5646305630816e1ee196

Git reports a "detached HEAD". This is expected: the checkout now sits on that commit instead of on a branch.

Step 4. Start Julia from the terminal.

julia

Step 5. In the Julia session, activate the environment of the checkout. 

using Pkg
Pkg.activate("/path/to/CMBLensing.jl")

Step 6. In the same session, install the dependencies of the checkout, then the three extra packages the data generators load.

Pkg.instantiate()
Pkg.add(["PythonCall", "PythonPlot", "NPZ"])
Pkg.precompile()

CMBLensing itself is not added: the activated environment is CMBLensing, and Julia refuses to add a package to its own environment.

Step 7. Still in the same session, check that the checkout loads, then leave Julia.

using CMBLensing
exit()

Step 8. Tell the test scripts where the checkout is. They read the path from an environment variable and pass it to juliacall, which activates the same environment as step 5.

On Linux and macOS, add the following line to the end of the file ~/.bashrc (or ~/.zshrc if your shell is zsh), so that every new terminal has the variable set:

export CMBLENSING_JL_PATH=/path/to/CMBLensing.jl

Then load it into the terminal you already have open:

source ~/.bashrc

Running the export line directly in a terminal also works, but only for that terminal: the variable is gone once it is closed.

On Windows, store the variable permanently with the command below, then close and reopen the terminal:

setx CMBLENSING_JL_PATH "C:\path\to\CMBLensing.jl"

If juliaup also has a newer Julia installed, juliacall picks the newest one rather than your default, and the 1.11 environment of steps 5 and 6 then fails to load (Artifact "LLVMExtra" was not found). Point juliacall at the 1.11 executable the same way:

export PYTHON_JULIAPKG_EXE="$(julia +1.11 -e 'print(joinpath(Sys.BINDIR, "julia"))')"

Step 9. From the root of the CMBLensing.py repository, regenerate all of the Julia data.

python tests/generate_julia_data/generate_all.py

To regenerate the data of a single test instead, run its generator on its own:

python tests/generate_julia_data/generate_lensing.py

To regenerate the data and run the tests in one command:

pytest --generate

docs.title: Confirming the checkout works
docs.text:
After regenerating the data, run the MAP estimate comparison:

pytest tests/test_map_joint.py

It writes its plots into three folders, one per kind of data:

tests/test_generated_figures/map_joint/intensity_only/
tests/test_generated_figures/map_joint/polarization_only/
tests/test_generated_figures/map_joint/intensity_and_polarization/

A Julia result that is NaN or all zeros typically means one of three things:

  • the environment of the checkout was not activated (steps 5 and 8),
  • the Julia version is not 1.11 (step 2),
  • the checkout is not at the commit above (step 3).

docs.title: Submitting a pull request
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository and create a branch off master.
  2. Keep each pull request focused on one change.
  3. Run the tests that cover the code you touched.
  4. If your change affects numerical results, say in the pull request description how you checked it (for example against CMBLensing.jl or direct CAMB).
  5. If you change the commands or the outputs of a pipeline, update the matching page in docs/ too.
  6. Open the pull request against master and describe what it changes and why.

The LCDM sampler, the Fisher forecast and the noise measurement modules have no tests yet, so contributions there are especially welcome.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
There is no automatic formatter, so please follow these conventions:

  • Write plain, readable code, with variable names that follow the physics (cphi, nphi, cl_tt, ...). Readability should not cost performance.
  • If a standard library (numpy, scipy, jax, the Python standard library) already does the job, use it instead of writing your own version.
  • No magic numbers: give every constant a name, and put the widely used ones in cmb_lensing/constants.py.
  • Keep the code lean: do not add defensive input checks or machinery that the computation does not need.

docs.title: Building the documentation
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs Material. The pages are in the folder docs/ and the navigation is in mkdocs.yml.

mkdocs serve            #local preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict   #run this before pushing

The site is redeployed automatically on every push to master.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install it in editable mode from the repository root (the folder holding pyproject.toml):

git clone https://github.com/zaneblood1/CMBLensing.py.git
cd CMBLensing.py

This pulls in JAX (pinned to jax == jaxlib == 0.9.2), Flax, CAMB, NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib. Python 3.10 or newer is required. JAX is configured for float64 globally on import.

Optional extras:
